author.name: Dorothea Frede
author.tradition: Anglo-German analytic ancient philosophy; trained in the Tübingen/Göttingen post-war ancient-philosophy tradition; closely aligned in this period with the Anglo-American Aristotle revival represented in the Nussbaum-Rorty Essays volume

essay_title: The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle
publication: in Martha C. Nussbaum & Amélie O. Rorty (eds.), Essays on Aristotle's De Anima, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1992, pp. 279-295 (chapter 15 of the volume; PDF body pages numbered 279-295)
ocr_confidence: high; offprint cleanly typeset with consistent italics for Greek terms (phantasia, phantasma, aisthesis, noesis, doxa, eidolopoiein, etc.); Bekker references legible (occasional OCR glitches around superscript columns 'a/b' rendered as straight quotes, e.g. 427b15 may appear as 427'b15 or 427bi5; corrected silently in the analysis); footnote numerals and chapter cross-references intact
special_features: Three numbered Roman-headed sections: I. Problems with a Unified Concept of Phantasia; II. Phantasia as Synthesizer; III. Thought and the Objects of Sense-Perception
50 footnotes spread across the short 17-page essay — Frede is footnote-dense

Self-described 'minimal account' of phantasia in DA III.3 (p. 280), confining itself to two functions: (a) synthesis/retention of sense-perceptions, and (b) bridging of thought to objects of sense-perception

Signature thesis stated at p. 286 (paraphrased): Aristotle does not treat phantastike as a separate soul-faculty but as a phenomenon supervening on sense-perception; with no faculty governing images as such, decayed/doubtful images can only be checked by returning to sense-experience itself.
Closing footnote 50 acknowledges Wedin (1988) as reaching 'similar results but much more extensive and technically refined' — placing Frede in dialogue with Wedin's monograph

Cites the cluster's contemporary authors: Nussbaum (1978) De Motu Animalium and (1985 essay volume context); Schofield (1979 'Aristotle on the Imagination'); Watson (1982); Modrak (1986, 1987a); Sorabji (1971, 1974); Kahn (1966); Cashdollar (1973); Burnyeat (1981); Barnes (1975, 1979b); Hamlyn (Aristotle 1968); Ross (Aristotle 1961a); does NOT cite White (1985) — likely because White appeared in the same year as the writing of this volume and was published in a Canadian philosophy journal outside the Anglo-Aristotle mainstream
Engages Kant explicitly (Critique of Pure Reason A 190 ff., B 154) on synthesis of the manifold and on thinking a line by drawing one — Frede draws Kant-Aristotle parallels at two crucial junctures
Defends a dualist reading of Aristotle's psychology AGAINST Modrak's (1987a) unified-consciousness reading

section_structure.heading: I. Problems with a Unified Concept of Phantasia
section_structure.summary: Diagnoses the translational and conceptual difficulties of phantasia. The word does 'triple duty' designating capacity, activity/process, and product (cf. English 'sight'). Aristotle himself uses phantasma for the product and phantastikon for the capacity (DA 432a31). The active sense (eidolopoiein, DA 427b18-20) is ruled out at 428a2 as kata metaphoran (footnote 3). Frede focuses on the passive/medial sense: 'appearance' as the central meaning. She then surveys the seeming inconsistencies of DA III.3: phantasia as necessary condition of thought (427b15) vs. phantasiai as mere mostly-false after-images (428a11-16); the chapter's repetitions, postponed definition (428b10ff), and the abandonment of the object-defines-faculty methodology of book II. Frede announces a 'minimal account' confined to two functions: synthesis/retention and the bridging of thought to sensible objects. She closes the section with Aristotle's final definition: phantasia is a motion that does not happen without sense-perception but comes to be as the result of the activity of sense-perception, and is like perception (428b11-15; 429a1; Somn. Vig. 459a17). Phantasia 'does not have a faculty of its own but is parasitic on sense-perception.'

section_structure.heading: II. Phantasia as Synthesizer
section_structure.summary: Argues that phantasia performs the synthesis-of-the-manifold work that sense-perception cannot do because perception is narrowly confined to its present object. Frede invokes Kant's example (Critique of Pure Reason A 190 ff.) of looking up and down a house: the overall impression of all the books on her shelves (including those behind her back) is already a phantasia, a synthesis of present and recently-past perceptions. The 'common sense' (inner sense, koine aisthesis) is not strictly above the senses but their centre/coordinator; its imprints, like external sense-imprints, last only as long as the perception. What lingers when the eye averts is already a phantasia. This explains why DA 425b23 calls these imprints 'perceptions and imaginations' and why 428b27 says we have phantasiai already while sense-perception is in operation. Frede defends a tight causal link between perception and after-image (a causal gap would be unbridgeable). She extends phantasia to all sense modalities (hearing melodies, smell, touch, taste). Phantasiai can be separated from their origin (perceptions cannot) and give us a coherent picture spanning time. Their truth-value can change and decay because there is 'no special faculty in the soul that keeps them in order' — they drift, dream, delude, become incorrigible (the sun's apparent foot-wide size, DA 428b3, Insomn. 458b28). Phantasia thus furnishes the 'field of vision,' the wider picture, the cognition of attributes (sumbebekota, DA 402b23) without which science would be empty dialectic. It functions as the counterpart of doxa (Insomn. 462a1).

section_structure.heading: III. Thought and the Objects of Sense-Perception
section_structure.summary: Examines phantasia's bridging role between sense-perception and nous. Aristotle's initial sharp dichotomy (nous receives intelligible forms; aisthesis receives perceptible forms, 432a2) is later softened: we only get to know intelligibles through sensibles (432a3 ff). Imagination establishes the connection. The need is twofold: practical and theoretical reasoning both require phantasmata. (1) Practical: action requires envisaging something as good or bad (DA 431a14-17; 433b12, 28); 'thinking of something terrible alone does not move us' (432b29); the World-Trade-Center-plank example shows that geometric reason alone cannot stir us to action. Aristotle subdivides into deliberative/calculative phantasia (bouleutike or logistike, 433b29, 434a5-7) for human decision-making vs. non-rational phantasia shared with animals; even worms have phantasia 'indefinitely' (433b31). (2) Theoretical: nous always 'thinks the forms in the images' (431b2) — like Kant, Aristotle holds we cannot think of a line without drawing one in our mind (B 154). Phantasmata are flexible (sense-perceptions are not), enriched by repeated observations, providing generalization. Their inaccuracy is in fact their advantage: it yields the 'standardized picture' (cf. Freudenthal 1863's 'Verallgemeinerung durch Denkthätigkeit'). Phantasia is crucial for epagoge (APo. II.19, 99b36-100b9). Frede then poses the unity-of-consciousness question and DECLINES a Modrak-style integration: Aristotle's strict separation of aisthetikon and noeton — confining memory and dreams entirely to the sensible side (Mem. 450a12-14; Insomn. 458b10, 459a8) — means no real fusion was conceivable to him. Frede defends Aristotle's dualism. The closing pages defend phantasia as a single unified phenomenon (against Schofield 1979's 'loose-knit family concept'): the causal account is uniform (motions in the soul caused by sense-perceptions), and Aristotle's 'insistence on their sensory nature' indicates a unitary sensory phenomenon.

outline: Cluster 1 (PDF 1, book 279, §I opening): Frede opens by noting that phantasia does 'triple duty': capacity, activity/process, and product. English 'sight' shares the same range (the capacity to see, the seeing, and what is seen) without confusion. Aristotle uses phantasma for the product and phantastikon (DA 432a31) for the capacity. Frede invokes the etymological derivation from phainesthai/phantazesthai and proposes 'appearance' as the central meaning to which all three functions relate: (i) the capacity to experience an appearance, (ii) the on-going appearance itself, (iii) what appears. She notes a further wrinkle: sometimes 'imagination' (eidolopoiein, the active creation of an appearance) is more adequate, related to 'appearance' as active to passive.

Cluster 2 (PDF 1-2, book 279-280): Aristotle distinguishes (with Greek's help) phantasia from phantasma (mere appearance/phantom) and phenomenon (real appearance). Aristotle uses phantasia in all senses but most often in the passive/medial sense; the active eidolopoiein use (DA 427b18-20) is ruled out by 428a2 as kata metaphoran (footnote 3: it never recurs in DA, does not suit the cognitive use, fails the soon-to-come definition of phantasia as motion-caused-by-perception). Aristotle's insouciance about meanings does not imply confusion: he carefully distinguishes capacity, activity, and product throughout the psychological writings.

Cluster 3 (PDF 2, book 280, opening problem): The crucial question — what kinds of 'appearances' does Aristotle have in mind and why a special capacity for them? DA III.3 is confusing at first sight: phantasia is a necessary condition of thought ('there is no supposition without it,' 427b15), yet phantasiai are mere often-false after-images guiding animals (which lack reason) and humans when disturbed by passion/disease/sleep (428a11-16, 429a4-8). The discussion of recent years (Nussbaum 1978, Schofield 1979, Watson 1982, Modrak 1986/1987a — footnote 5) about phantasia's cognitive value cannot be done full justice. Frede confines herself to a 'minimal account' of phantasia's role in DA III.3 and how it is borne out elsewhere.

Cluster 4 (PDF 2, book 280-281, problems with III.3): Aristotle in III.3 displays the 'untidy-genius syndrome.' Repetitions and inconsistencies abound: definition postponed to 428b10ff; criteria first introduced to distinguish perception/thought/phantasia are circumstantial, soon modified or contradicted. Sense-perception first differentiated as always true (phantasia usually false, 428a11), then only 'specific' perceptions almost always true while perceptions of common and accidental objects can be false (428b18ff). Phantasia first separated from sense and thought (427b14), then subsumed under noein and called the counterpart of hupolepsis (427b27). Phantasia first 'up to us' (we imagine what we please), then not (dreams aren't up to us), and phantasiai true or false (else they wouldn't mislead). All animals first said to have perception but not phantasia, then this is modified (DA III.11).

Cluster 5 (PDF 2-3, book 281, methodological surprise): What surprises more than the inconsistencies is Aristotle's reliance on indirect evidence — he spends time pointing out what perception/phantasia/thought have IN COMMON rather than distinguishing them by their specific objects. This violates the object-defines-faculty methodology of DA II (415a20; 418a7ff; EN 1139a8-11). The reason becomes clear at the final definition: Aristotle wants to lead us to agree that phantasia and sense-perception must be DIFFERENT, precisely because in his final definition there is NO separate capacity in the soul and NO separate objects for phantasia. The definition: 'Phantasia is a motion that does not happen without sense-perception but comes to be as the result of the activity of sense-perception and is like perception' (428b11-15; 429a1; Somn. Vig. 459a17). Phantasia has no faculty of its own; it is 'parasitic on sense-perception.'

Cluster 6 (PDF 3, book 281-282, truth-status of phantasia): The truth/falsity of phantasia depends on the character of the corresponding sense-perception. Phantasia following perception of the special object (idion, e.g. colour for vision) is true as long as the perception lasts, but can become false once perception is over. Phantasia following common-object or accidental perception can be false even with the perception (428b25-30). Aristotle gives no causal connection between sense-perception and phantasiai, nor a phenomenological description distinguishing them. It looks as if phantasiai have been degraded to mere epiphenomena, the lingering after-images of sensations.

Cluster 7 (PDF 3, book 282, tension): This 'mere after-image' impression squares with the assertion that we speak of appearance when we lack clear perception (428a12-15) and the earlier 'as in a picture' remark (427b23-4). But it conflicts with the assertion that without phantasiai there can be no thought (427b16) and with the cognitive function under noein (427b27ff). What kind of noesis and krisis can phantasia perform if it is utterly dependent on perception, a mere after-image or unclear appearance? Frede announces her programmatic answer: to look beyond III.3 and identify two functions of phantasia that fill the gap — (a) synthesis and retention of sense-perceptions, (b) applying thought to objects of sense-perception.

Cluster 8 (PDF 3-4, book 282-283, §II opens, the anatomy of perception): Sense-perception is the interaction between the object and the actualized capacity. The sense-organ is affected by the perceptible form of the object without the matter (ton aistheton eidon aneu tes hules, II.12, 424a17): the wax-receiving-the-seal-without-the-iron simile. The soul receives the colour without the coloured surface. Perception is not merely passive but also a 'critical faculty' that 'judges' (krinei) what it receives. This 'critical' function is the discernment of the specific objects of the sense (426b20; 427a1, 9); not explicit predication (animals have no opinions) but the implicit recognition that animals exhibit (a dog recognizes its master without saying 'this is the master').

Cluster 9 (PDF 4, book 283, narrowness of perception): Cutting a long story short, perception is narrowly limited to what is immediately perceived (417a24-8; 425b6ff; APo. 87b28-39). Aristotle has no 'panoramic view of a whole situation,' no 'field of vision.' Looking over books on shelves: there is always just the piecemeal vision of this or that coloured object; the overall impression of all books (including those behind one's back) is already a phantasia — a synthesis of what I perceive now and what I perceived seconds ago. Kant (Critique of Pure Reason A 190 ff.) describes such synthesis when looking up and down a house (footnote 16). The synthesis-of-the-manifold motif is Kantian.

Cluster 10 (PDF 4, book 283-284, common sense): The 'common sense' (also called inner sense or first sense, koine aisthesis) has integrative roles. It receives all sensory information and has a kind of 'authority' over the different senses (DA 426b17-29, elaborated in Parva Naturalia; cf. Kahn 1966). One might assign synthesizing to the inner sense rather than to phantasia. The inner sense does receive and discern different sensations simultaneously (Sens. 7) — koina aistheta (motion seen and felt), accidental perception (the white thing as the son of Diares). But the inner sense is not above the senses; it is only their CENTRE where perceptions converge. Its imprints, qua sense-imprints, last only as long as perception itself. Therefore what lingers when the eye averts is already a phantasia.

Cluster 11 (PDF 4, book 284, the simultaneity of perception and phantasia): This explains why Aristotle at 425b23 calls these imprints 'perceptions and imaginations,' and why he claims at 428b27 that we have phantasiai already while sense-perception is still in operation. A simpler explanation — that unclear perceptions can be classified as appearances — does not exhaust the matter. Without simultaneity there would be an unbridgeable causal gap: once perception is gone, what would give rise to the phantasma? The residual motion 'has a life of its own.' Aristotle is not explicit about when/where the changes take place or when perception turns into phantasia. Somn. Vig. 459b5ff shows that he assumes the residual motions have complexity and duration, often unperceived because dominated by stronger immediate impressions (en bathei kai epipoles 459b7).

Cluster 12 (PDF 4-5, book 284-285, memory and phantasia): Why does Aristotle not ascribe all after-images to memory? Because memory (De Memoria) is the act of remembering a past experience qua past. A memory of a sunset only counts as such if it is OF a particular past sunset. Free-floating mental items contemplating sunsets in general are mere images, while memories are images retained from the past WITH the association of the time-lapse (Mem. 450a21ff '... prosaisthanesthai hoti proteron'). Phantasmata need not have precise correspondence to their object (Insomn. 460b6 says small resemblance of the pathe suffices); the image-theory does not require exactness. Phantasmata are not confined to visual images: hearing melodies, smell, touch, taste all yield phantasmata. We lack a verb covering all these. 'Recall' may be the best general term, with the caveat it need not be intentional.

Cluster 13 (PDF 5, book 285, separability of phantasia from origin): Phantasiai can be SEPARATED from their origin (perceptions cannot). They give us a coherent picture transcending immediate perception. Imagination supplies the impression of CHANGE OVER TIME — eyes gliding over objects, ears following a melody. Strictly, the eye perceives only one object at a time; animals without phantasia would get a sequence of incoherent imprints. Because phantasiai change in quality and object once separated from their origin, Aristotle declares most of them false and misleading: there is no faculty in the soul controlling them, no 'keeper of order,' so they drift in and out of consciousness, reappear in dreams, delude us in fever.

Cluster 14 (PDF 5, book 286, THE SUPERVENIENCE THESIS — the signature passage): Frede's central thesis is asserted: Aristotle declines to treat the phantastike as a separate soul-faculty and instead regards it as a phenomenon supervening on perception; since no faculty governs images as such, the only recourse when image-quality decays or truth-status becomes doubtful is to return to sense-experience itself (paraphrased; cf. book p. 286). Where the senses themselves are not decisive (the 'incorrigible' apparent size of the sun, DA 428b3), reason must find OTHER means of deciding (footnote 25: Insomn. 458b28 on incorrigibility; 461b30 on the control of phantasiai).

Cluster 15 (PDF 5, book 286, field-of-vision argument): There is little direct evidence for Frede's claim that Aristotle designed phantasia to constitute a 'field of vision' or coherent trains of events; she has given reasons rather than evidence. What speaks for it: (1) the perseverance assigned to phantasiai (to emmenein, DA 429a4; Insomn. 460b1-3) fits supplying after-images, memory, dreams (Insomn. 460b27); (2) phantasia provides cognition of attributes (DA 402b23 sumbebekota), without which science is 'empty dialectic'; (3) the vexed duplication of perception and phantasia in the presence of the object — defended here as necessary for coherence and continuity of perception, not just for causal continuity. Phantasia delivers the 'wider picture' that simultaneous reports of different senses cannot.

Cluster 16 (PDF 5-6, book 286, sun's-size example): DA 448a13 ('one sees the sun or a four-cubit rod, but it is not apparent how large they are' — all' ou phainetai hosa estin) is explained: estimating size is what one expects from phantasia as a kind of 'comparative seeing' (comparing the sun with tree-tops or chimney-pots). Phantasia gives a sensory representation of a state of affairs going beyond simultaneous reports of the senses; it is often depicted as the counterpart of doxa (Insomn. 462a1: 'not only does it appear so but it also seems so'; cf. 461b1). Footnote 26 disputes Schofield (1979 ch. 14, pp. 251-2, 253-4, 267-8): Schofield's reading of phantasia as a sceptical, cautious, non-committing phainetai is 'one-sided' and ignores its roles in memory, thinking, decision-making, and the causal account of trustworthiness.

Cluster 17 (PDF 6, book 287, transition to §III): Why so few traces of a 'wider' use of phantasia outside practical reason? Frede speculates that Aristotle is not interested in describing observations of trains of events but in things and their properties (DA 402b27). She then turns to the second function of phantasia: bridging thought to sensible objects.

Cluster 18 (PDF 6, book 287, §III opens): All thinking depends on phantasiai (DA 427b16; cf. 403a8-9). This is claimed without elaboration at first, then explained in the following chapters. The diagnostic/interpretive function of perception+phantasia (including common-objects: size, number, motion, rest, shape; and accidental objects, what the underlying thing is) suggests that the senses and phantasia present the mind with 'finished products,' matters of fact, states of affairs ('I see the pale thing as the son of Cleon').

Cluster 19 (PDF 6, book 287-288, seeing-as): But this seeing-as need not be explicit or propositional, since perception and imagination are common to humans and animals; the seeing-as cannot be explicitly predicative. This is why Aristotle says animals have phantasiai but not opinions or convictions, no pisteis (428a21). The diagnostic function is implicit recognition.

Cluster 20 (PDF 6, book 288, what phantasia delivers to the intellect): If phantasiai are not per se diagnostic, what is their relationship to the intellect? III.3 only mentions that without phantasia there could be no suppositions; soon after, the kinds of supposition are: episteme, doxa, phronesis, and their opposites (427b25). Any thinking that assumes a state of affairs. The intellect (DA III.4) is defined narrowly: it receives intelligible forms without matter; it is to the intelligible as perception is to the sensible. The intellect has nothing to do with the body; it thinks by itself (429b9) once it has grasped immaterial forms.

Cluster 21 (PDF 6, book 288, the rigid dichotomy): Aristotle limits the intellect exclusively to thinking essences (429b10ff) and confines sense-perception to the material aspect. He concludes: 'just as things are separable from matter, so are the objects of the intellect' (429b21). The dualism: nous is its objects when thinking immaterial things, since it is like a clean slate (429a21-3; 430a1). The intellect is the form of forms; sense-perception is the form of perceptibles (432a2). This strict separation is asserted repeatedly.

Cluster 22 (PDF 6-7, book 288-289, softening of the dichotomy): Despite the rigid dichotomy, the autonomy of the intellect is incomplete (432a3ff). We only get to know intelligible forms of material entities (virtually everything except mind itself) THROUGH knowledge of sensibles. Sense-perception is indispensable at least for learning, even for abstract sciences like geometry. The intellect thinks 'quite different subject-matters' beyond essences (429a23 'what it thinks and assumes'); it discursively thinks about concrete sensibles (430a31ff 'e.g. Cleon is pale or was or will be,' 426b22, 31; 427a9). HERE is where imagination comes in: it establishes the connection between intellect and its sensible objects.

Cluster 23 (PDF 7, book 289, the two-sided need for phantasmata): The need for images is twofold: practical and theoretical reasoning. (1) Practical reasoning: all activities, whether based on non-rational or rational desire, presuppose envisaging something as good or bad, to be pursued or avoided. The necessary condition is that the soul has certain phantasmata (431a14-17): the image of a future good or bad (433b12, 28).

Cluster 24 (PDF 7, book 289, why intellect alone won't do): Why doesn't intellect suffice for figuring out what is good/bad? And why doesn't sense-perception establish the connection where sensible objects are needed? Once again: the narrow confinement of intellect and sense-perception to their respective objects. The intellect by itself can only think the non-sensible intelligible forms; but it needs sensible images to decide whether something is desirable. It must envisage concrete situations containing material objects. Sense-perception is strictly limited to what is given to the senses NOW. Sense-perceptions in the wider sense (Aristotle's looser usage) are already phantasmata in precise speech (footnote 35). There can be no sense-perceptions of FUTURE goods/evils; all sensible projections come from imagination. Phantasmata 'serve as perceptions' to the rational soul (431a14).

Cluster 25 (PDF 7, book 289-290, the worthwhile-aim example and the beacon): To make a decision Frede has to create for herself the appearance of a future good (433a14). Aristotle's beacon example: when one sees fire and that it moves, one realizes the enemy is there (sense-perception and calculation do the job). But the soul also calculates 'through images and thoughts as if seeing' (hosper horon, 431b7) and deliberates about future in relation to present. The soul would not be moved toward anything if it could not envisage it concretely. Aristotle later puts it: 'thinking of something terrible alone does not move us' (432b29).

Cluster 26 (PDF 7, book 290, the World-Trade-Center example): Frede's striking modern example: her geometric mind tells her she can pass along any path wide enough for her two feet; but the depiction of walking over a plank from one tower of the World Trade Center to the other tells her this is an absolute pheukton, a thing to avoid. The example illustrates that the cognitive force motivating action requires phantasmatic envisaging, not merely abstract geometric reasoning.

Cluster 27 (PDF 7, book 290, deliberative/calculative phantasia): Most of DA III.7-9 is on phantasia's role in practical reasoning. Aristotle subdivides between bouleutike/logistike phantasia (calculative/deliberative, in human decision-making) and non-rational phantasia (shared with animals) (footnote 36: 433b29, 434a5-7). The subdivision does not introduce two separate capacities suddenly; the bouleutike/logistike phantasia must supply concrete visions illustrating what is desirable. Without phantasia, desire would be without direction; hence even primitive animals (worms) have phantasia 'indefinitely' (433b31ff). Phantasia plays a crucial role in MA (footnote 37: 701b18 'phantasia and thinking have the power of the actual thing').

Cluster 28 (PDF 7-8, book 290, theoretical reasoning's need for images): (2) Theoretical reasoning also needs images (431b2; 432a3ff). Given Aristotle's account of learning, we could never attain the essences of things without starting from their appearances. But not just learning — ALL thinking depends on sensible images. Despite the initial rigid dichotomy (431b20-432a2), Aristotle later concedes that intelligible objects of all thought, even in abstract sciences, are contained in sensible objects (432a3-9 'ta te en aphairesei legomena kai hosa ton aistheton hexeis kai pathe').

Cluster 29 (PDF 8, book 290-291, the most-important point — the Kantian parallel): General conclusion: 'one could not get to know them nor understand them without sense-perception' (oute me aisthanomenos methen outhen an mathoi oude xunheie). More importantly, one cannot even THINK (contemplate) without images: 'hotan te theorei, ananke hama phantasma ti theorein' (432a8-9). Images, 'like sense-perceptions except without (sensible) matter,' provide the substrate of all thought, so that reason 'thinks the forms in the images' (431b2). Aristotle, like Kant, wants to say we cannot think of a line without drawing one in our mind (B 154). Even when he denies the identity of objects of thought and objects of imagination (432a12-14), he insists that whenever we think of the form of something we have something like a Gestalt of it in mind.

Cluster 30 (PDF 8, book 291, Gestalt and the house example): Frede doesn't turn Aristotle into a Gestalt psychologist, but his basic idea must be that comprehension of formal definition is not enough. Thinking of a house: it's not enough to think 'a shelter against destruction'; thinking of a circle: not enough as 'the common locus of all points having the same distance from a central point.' Without Gestalt we couldn't recognize exemplars or do geometric constructions (which depend on seeing relevant relationships).

Cluster 31 (PDF 8, book 291, generalization through phantasmata): Objects of imagination render an object for knowledge when there is no direct perception. Sense-perception is narrowly limited to the particular object directly under inspection (417b22-8). The scientist studying leopards needs more than the view of THIS or THAT leopard spotted in some particular way — a picture of leopards in general, their specific spottedness, abstracted from individuals. Phantasmata are flexible and enriched by repeated observations; immediate sense-perceptions cannot be. The disadvantage of inaccuracy turns into an advantage (Ross 1961a 39 in footnote 40: Aristotle 'on the whole does not regard it as a valuable faculty but as a disability'; Freudenthal 1863 in footnote 41: 'Verallgemeinerung durch Denkthätigkeit'). Phantasmata supply a 'standardized picture' of states of affairs.

Cluster 32 (PDF 8, book 291, sun's-size again and decision-making): The sun's apparent foot-diameter illustrates: when I reflect on the real size of the sun, I reflect not on this particular vision but on the 'overall vision' of the sun and why this must be a delusion. Phantasmata also figure in decision-making: Aristotle mentions a 'merger' of different phantasiai into one image allowing comparison of relative goodness/badness of possible ends (434a9). They figure in science: the scientist asking about straight objects looking bent in water asks why straight objects in general do so (induction, epagoge — footnote 42 on APo. II.19).

Cluster 33 (PDF 8, book 292, phantasia and APo. II.19): APo. II.19 (the locus classicus on sense-to-science) doesn't mention phantasia by name, but the kind of aisthesis there really consists in phantasiai. Only retained perceptions (for animals having mone of their perceptions) lead to memory and experience (99b36-100b9). Aristotle uses aisthesis here in its wider sense — emphasizing perception of the universal, not the particular. Only collected phantasiai of many sense-perceptions lead to the sight of the universal feature in the particular. Aristotle may have found it cumbersome to introduce phantasia in APo. II.19; it's enough that the basic information comes through the senses.

Cluster 34 (PDF 8, book 292, summary of the linking role): Upshot: phantasia plays a crucial cognitive role in BOTH practical and theoretical thinking by supplying the necessary link between sensible and intelligible. The link is necessary because most objects of science are 'enmattered' and because our thinking cannot be entirely abstract — it always needs a kind of Gestalt.

Cluster 35 (PDF 8-9, book 292-293, the unity-of-consciousness question — Frede vs. Modrak): A final question: does the integrative function of phantasia permit ascribing to Aristotle a unity-of-consciousness conception comprising senses and intellect, as some commentators (Modrak 1987a, footnote 44) have assumed? Frede is cautious. Aristotle's scientific optimism (mind progresses from sense-perception to knowledge; sufficient empirical study yields recognition of general features; APo. II.19 100a1 ff: 'when many such things come about, then a difference comes about'). Yet Aristotle in Metaph. A 1-2 says everybody has perceptions (rhadion kai ouden sophon, 982a12) but knowledge of reasons is the privilege of the sophoi and most difficult to achieve. Empirical knowledge through phantasia alone does not lead securely from 'fact that' to 'reason why' (footnote 45: Burnyeat 1981, 114 on 'intellectual habituation').

Cluster 36 (PDF 9, book 293-294, Frede's anti-Modrak position): Apart from continuity, there are indications that Aristotle consciously preserved the SEPARATION of sensible and intelligible (aistheta and noeta), despite phantasia's mediation. This forbids assuming a unity of consciousness based on perception. The definition of memory and of dreams confines these to the SENSIBLE side. Though Aristotle grants we have opinions in dreams (458b10), he attributes dreams exclusively to the aisthetikon, 'in so far as it is phantastikon' (459a8). This leaves the status of opinions in dreams unexplained, but it suggests Aristotle saw a need to assign psychic phenomena either to sensible or intelligible domain: no real fusion was conceivable to him.

Cluster 37 (PDF 9, book 293-294, no intellectual memory): Same for memory: memories are revivals of phantasiai of past experiences. Knowledge is 'remembered' only accidentally (Mem. 450a12-14): we remember WHEN and HOW we first learned Pythagoras' theorem, not the theorem itself. The decision to locate memory with the sensible faculties FORBIDS Aristotle to admit a kind of intellectual memory. This means, as with dreams, the status of beliefs embedded in sensory memories remains unaccounted for. Footnote 47 emphasizes: in Insomn. Aristotle distinguishes between opinions in dreams and opinions in sleep besides dreams (458b15), defining dreams as phantasmata in sleep (459a19).

Cluster 38 (PDF 9, book 294, why Aristotle preserved dualism): If Aristotle wants to keep the faculties separate, regarding phantasia only as a link CONFINED to the sensory side, he must have had reasons. (a) He did not want to accept physical impact on the functioning of the intellect per se (which would be implied by more than accidental connection). (b) He did not want to give up the link between the best part in us and the only divinity he recognizes: the pure active mind (408b18-29; Metaph. 983a6-7).

Cluster 39 (PDF 9, book 294, dualism not incoherent): The dualism Frede maintains for Aristotle does not make his philosophy of mind incoherent. It imports awkwardnesses unavoidable for any metaphysics distinguishing the corporeal and incorporeal in a strong sense. Aristotle must have hoped his conception of phantasia would help overcome that awkwardness.

Cluster 40 (PDF 9, book 294, against the matter-form metaphor for phantasia/nous): The relationship between phantasia (or aisthesis in wider sense) and nous has recently been likened to matter and form (Modrak 1987a 123-4, 215 n.29). As metaphor, acceptable — senses deliver material reason works on. But dangerous because it suggests a NECESSARY relationship. Unlike matter, phantasiai exist by themselves, need not be 'informed' by thought. More importantly, phantasiai are sometimes recalcitrant and RESIST 'information' — the sun-foot-wide example from Insomn. 458b28: even when persons know the facts perfectly well, the sun still appears a foot wide. Phantasiai remain 'phenomena in their own right.'

Cluster 41 (PDF 9, book 294-295, the unity-vs-family-concept question): Has Frede treated phantasia as a unified concept justifiably, or is it rather a 'more or less coherent family of psychic phenomena, a loose-knit family concept' (Schofield 1979, 108, 110)? If one excludes the metaphoric 'phantasizing' sense, at least the CAUSAL ACCOUNT is uniform: all phantasiai are motions in the soul caused by sense-perceptions. They are sensory images/imprints existing independently of their source. Their history may vary (immediate awareness vs. long-term storage), as may function and occasion (dreams, hallucinations, memory, thoughts, decisions), as may their character (clear/confused, simple/complex, true/false). Despite this range, Aristotle's 'insistence on their sensory nature' indicates he regarded them as a 'unitary phenomenon in the soul, as sensory appearances.'

Cluster 42 (PDF 9, book 295, Wedin acknowledgment): Final footnote 50: 'For an interpretation that reaches similar results but is much more extensive and technically refined cf. Wedin (1988). A discussion of his very rich investigations would exceed the limits of this article.' Frede thus signals her position is convergent with Wedin's Mind and Imagination in Aristotle (1988) without arguing through it.

concepts.label: phantasia as supervenient phenomenon
concepts.gloss: Frede's signature thesis: phantasia is NOT a separate faculty of the soul but a phenomenon that supervenes on sense-perception; there is no faculty in charge of images as such (DA 432a31, 459a17, 460b27)

concepts.label: phantasia 'parasitic' on sense-perception
concepts.gloss: Frede's metaphor at p. 281: phantasia does not have a faculty of its own but is 'parasitic' on sense-perception; perception is its causal source

concepts.label: phantasia as synthesizer
concepts.gloss: Frede's first thesis-function: phantasia performs the synthesis-of-the-manifold work that piecemeal sense-perception cannot; supplies the 'field of vision' or 'wider picture'

concepts.label: phantasia as bridge between sensible and intelligible
concepts.gloss: Frede's second thesis-function: phantasia establishes the connection between the intellect and its sensible objects, in both practical and theoretical reasoning

concepts.label: decay/persistence of phantasmata (to emmenein)
concepts.gloss: The lingering, drifting after-images that may change in quality and truth-value once separated from their origin; DA 429a4, Insomn. 460b1-3

concepts.label: incorrigible appearance (the sun appearing a foot wide)
concepts.gloss: Insomn. 458b28: even when one knows perfectly well, the sun still appears a foot wide. Phantasmata can resist 'information' from reason; reason must turn to other means (DA 428b3)

concepts.label: denial of intellectual memory
concepts.gloss: Frede's anti-Modrak point: Aristotle locates memory exclusively in the sensitive faculty; knowledge is 'remembered' only accidentally (Mem. 450a12-14: we remember when/how we learned Pythagoras' theorem, not the theorem). No intellectual memory is admitted

concepts.label: dreams confined to aisthetikon qua phantastikon
concepts.gloss: Insomn. 459a8: dreams are attributed exclusively to the sensitive faculty 'in so far as it is phantastikon.' Opinions in dreams are left unexplained; the move signals Aristotle's refusal of fusion

concepts.label: calculative/deliberative phantasia (bouleutike/logistike)
concepts.gloss: DA 433b29, 434a5-7: subdivision distinguishing human deliberative phantasia from non-rational phantasia shared with animals. Not two separate capacities; provides concrete visions of what is desirable

concepts.label: phantasia 'indefinitely' in primitive animals
concepts.gloss: DA 433b31ff: even worms have a kind of notion of their aim in food-search; phantasia is required wherever desire is directed

concepts.label: Gestalt requirement for thinking
concepts.gloss: Frede's Kantian-flavored claim: even when Aristotle denies identity of objects of thought and imagination (432a12-14), he insists we have a Gestalt of what we think; we cannot think a line without drawing one in our mind (B 154; cf. 431b2)

concepts.label: phantasmata as 'standardized picture' for generalization
concepts.gloss: Phantasmata are flexible (sense-perceptions are not), enriched by repeated observations, allowing generalization. Their inaccuracy IS their advantage; cf. Freudenthal 1863 'Verallgemeinerung durch Denkthätigkeit'

concepts.label: phantasia as counterpart of doxa
concepts.gloss: Insomn. 462a1: 'not only does it appear so but it also seems so' (ou monon phaneitai alla kai dokei); phantasia gives sensory representation of states of affairs going beyond simultaneous reports of the senses

concepts.label: no panoramic field of vision in perception
concepts.gloss: Sense-perception is confined to its immediate object (417a24-8, 425b6ff, APo. 87b28-39); the overall impression of the room is already a phantasia. Frede invokes Kant's house example (A 190 ff)

concepts.label: phantasia as 'untidy-genius syndrome' in DA III.3
concepts.gloss: Frede's diagnostic name for the chapter's repetitions, postponed definition, modified criteria, and self-contradictions

concepts.label: minimal account of phantasia
concepts.gloss: Frede's methodological self-description: she confines herself to two functions (synthesis/retention; bridging) rather than attempting a complete reconstruction

concepts.label: phantasia as motion in the soul caused by perception
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's final definition: phantasia is a motion (kinesis) that does not happen without sense-perception but comes to be as a result of perception's activity (DA 428b11-15; 429a1; Somn. Vig. 459a17)

concepts.label: image-flexibility / 'merger' of phantasiai
concepts.gloss: DA 434a9: a 'merger' of different phantasiai into one image allows comparison of the relative goodness/badness of possible ends; cf. scientific generalization

concepts.label: phantasia and epagoge (induction)
concepts.gloss: APo. II.19, 99b36-100b9: though Aristotle doesn't name phantasia, the kind of aisthesis that leads from memory to experience to nous of first principles consists in phantasiai. Wider sense of aisthesis

concepts.label: dualism of aisthetikon and noeton preserved by Aristotle
concepts.gloss: Frede's anti-Modrak thesis: Aristotle consciously kept the sensible and intelligible separate; phantasia mediates BUT remains confined to the sensible side

readings.label: Phantasia is NOT a separate faculty but supervenes on sense-perception
readings.gloss: Frede's central and signature thesis. The phantastike is not listed among the soul's faculties (cf. DA 413a23-5, b12-13, 414b31-2); when Aristotle discusses it explicitly (432a31) he expresses doubt whether it is a separate faculty or only different in being (toi men einai... panton heteron). In Somn. Vig. 459a16, 458b30, 462a8 it is clear it is the SAME faculty as aisthesis, only the activity is different. There is no faculty in charge of images as such; when their quality decays or truth-status is doubtful, one can do no more than return to sense-experience itself.

readings.label: Phantasia performs TWO cognitive functions: synthesis/retention and bridging thought to sensibles
readings.gloss: Frede's 'minimal account' programmatic thesis. (a) Synthesis: phantasia supplies the field of vision, the wider picture, the change-over-time that piecemeal sense-perception cannot deliver — including coherent picture of attributes (sumbebekota, DA 402b23) without which science is 'empty dialectic.' (b) Bridging: phantasia establishes the connection between intellect (nous) and sensible objects, both for practical reasoning (envisaging future goods/evils, 431a14-17; 433b12, 28) and for theoretical reasoning (nous 'thinks the forms in the images,' 431b2; cf. 432a8-9 'hotan te theorei, ananke hama phantasma ti theorein').

readings.label: Aristotle preserves a strict dualism of aisthetikon/noeton AGAINST Modrak's unified-consciousness reading
readings.gloss: Frede's polemical anti-Modrak thesis. Despite phantasia's mediating role, Aristotle assigns memory and dreams entirely to the sensitive faculty (Mem. 450a12-14; Insomn. 459a8). He denies intellectual memory; knowledge is 'remembered' only accidentally. Phantasia is a link CONFINED to the sensory side. No 'real fusion' was conceivable to Aristotle. The matter-form metaphor for phantasia-nous is inadequate because phantasiai exist by themselves, need not be 'informed' by thought, and can RESIST information (the sun-foot-wide example, Insomn. 458b28). Aristotle's reasons: avoiding physical impact on intellect per se; preserving the link between the best part in us and the divine pure active mind (408b18-29).

readings.label: Phantasia is a UNIFIED concept (against Schofield's 'loose-knit family' reading)
readings.gloss: Frede defends the unity of phantasia as one concept covering all its applications. Though phantasiai range from clear/confused, simple/complex, true/false, and across dreams/hallucinations/memory/thoughts/decisions, the CAUSAL ACCOUNT is uniform: all phantasiai are motions in the soul caused by sense-perceptions. Aristotle's 'insistence on their sensory nature indicates that he regarded them, with good reasons, as a unitary phenomenon in the soul, as sensory appearances.' Against Schofield (1979 ch. 14 pp. 108, 110, 253, 256) who saw a 'loose-knit family concept' and against Schofield's reductive 'cautious phainetai' reading (footnote 26).

tensions.label: Phantasia as mere after-image vs phantasia as cognitively load-bearing
tensions.description: DA III.3 itself oscillates between treating phantasiai as 'mere after-images of sense-perception, often false ones' (428a11-16) that guide animals and disturbed humans, and asserting that 'there is no supposition without it' (427b15) and subsuming phantasia under noein as the counterpart of hupolepsis (427b27). Frede's 'minimal account' is her response: phantasia performs two cognitive functions (synthesis, bridging) WITHOUT being upgraded into a separate faculty.
tensions.frede_resolution: Phantasia is genuinely cognitive in its synthesizing/bridging roles but remains parasitic on perception. The cognitive functions do not require positing a separate faculty — supervenience is enough.

tensions.label: Rigid intellect/sense dichotomy vs phantasia's bridging role (Aristotelian dualism)
tensions.description: Aristotle's initial sharp dichotomy at DA 431b20-432a2 (intellect receives intelligible forms; sense-perception receives perceptible forms) is later softened (432a3ff: intelligibles only known through sensibles). Phantasia mediates. But does mediation collapse the dichotomy into a unified consciousness (Modrak 1987a) or merely link two distinct domains while preserving dualism (Frede)?
tensions.frede_resolution: Aristotle preserves dualism consciously. Phantasia is the link but remains CONFINED to the sensible side. Memory and dreams are entirely on the sensible side; no intellectual memory is admitted. Aristotle's reasons: avoiding physical impact on intellect per se; preserving link with divine active mind.

tensions.label: Unified concept vs loose-knit family of phantasiai
tensions.description: Schofield (1979) argues phantasia in Aristotle is at best a 'more or less coherent family of psychic phenomena, a loose-knit family concept' given the diverse phenomena (dreams, hallucinations, memory, thoughts, decisions; clear/confused; simple/complex; true/false). Frede defends unity.
tensions.frede_resolution: The CAUSAL ACCOUNT is uniform: all phantasiai are motions in the soul caused by sense-perceptions, sensory images existing independently of their source. Aristotle's 'insistence on their sensory nature' indicates a unitary phenomenon as sensory appearances.

tensions.label: Continuity vs gap between empirical knowledge (phantasia-driven) and knowledge of reasons (epistemic)
tensions.description: APo. II.19 portrays a continuous progress from sense-perception via memory and experience to nous of first principles (the routed-army simile). Yet Metaph. A 1-2 emphasizes that knowledge of reasons is the privilege of the sophoi, most difficult to achieve (982a12 rhadion kai ouden sophon). Does phantasia underwrite a CONTINUOUS or DISCONTINUOUS ascent?
tensions.frede_resolution: Phantasia delivers 'standardized pictures' good for generalization but does not by itself secure the move from 'fact that' to 'reason why.' Intellectual habituation (Burnyeat 1981) and a residual epistemic gap remain.

interlocutors.name: Martha C. Nussbaum
interlocutors.stance: extensive discussion of phantasia (1978 De Motu Animalium) as 'envisaging the good'; broadens phantasia to comprise all phenomena admitting interpretation in the wider sense
interlocutors.frede_position: criticizes Nussbaum for severing phantasia's ties to envisaging-with-perception; the broadened conception cannot explain why Aristotle assigns phantasia to aisthesis if perceptions are not involved; Nussbaum does not adequately explain why phantasia is in the wider sense she ascribes to it

interlocutors.name: Malcolm Schofield
interlocutors.stance: (1979) phantasia as 'sceptical, cautious, non-committing phainetai'; phantasia is a 'loose-knit family concept'
interlocutors.frede_position: rejects both: the cautious-phainetai reading is 'one-sided,' ignoring phantasia's role in memory/thinking/decision-making and the causal account; phantasia is a UNIFIED concept via the uniform causal account

interlocutors.name: Deborah K. W. Modrak
interlocutors.stance: (1986, 1987a) defends a unified concept of phantasia ('awareness of sensory content under non-conducive conditions') and a unified concept of consciousness comprising sense and intellect
interlocutors.frede_position: PRIMARY POLEMICAL TARGET. Modrak's reading of phantasia is untenable (limits aisthesis to veridical perceptions; misreads 428b18-25). Her unity-of-consciousness reading downplays Aristotelian dualism; her metaphors (phantasmata as 'vehicles for associations,' noeton as 'representation of occurrent phantasma') gloss over difficulties. Frede defends Aristotle's dualism against Modrak's unified reading

interlocutors.name: Michael Wedin
interlocutors.stance: (1988) Mind and Imagination in Aristotle: technically refined reconstruction reaching similar conclusions to Frede's
interlocutors.frede_position: approving alignment: 'an interpretation that reaches similar results but is much more extensive and technically refined cf. Wedin (1988); a discussion of his very rich investigations would exceed the limits of this article'

interlocutors.name: Gerard Watson
interlocutors.stance: (1982) defends coherence of DA III.3 by pointing to its anti-Platonic stance; discusses physiology of phantasia

nussbaum_white_comparison: Frede positions herself centrally between the cluster's two 1985 forerunners (PHX-01 Nussbaum and PHX-02 White), though her direct engagement with each is asymmetric. With NUSSBAUM (PHX-01), Frede is explicitly and substantively critical: she cites Nussbaum's 1978 De Motu Animalium repeatedly (footnotes 5, 23, 34) and accuses Nussbaum of 'broadening' phantasia so as to comprise all kinds of phenomena admitting interpretation in the wider sense ('envisaging the good,' Nussbaum 1978 p. 263), which 'tries as far as possible to sever the ties to envisaging' and fails to provide an adequate answer to the question why Aristotle assigns phantasia to aisthesis at all. For Frede, Nussbaum's reading evacuates phantasia of its essential perceptual grounding. Frede's counter-thesis — phantasia as supervenient phenomenon on sense-perception, parasitic on perception, with no faculty of its own — is structured as a corrective to Nussbaum's expansive practical-rational reading. With WHITE (PHX-02), Frede has no engagement at all: White 1985 is not in her bibliography. The non-citation is informative. White published in Dialogue (Canadian Philosophical Review) in 1985, the same year Nussbaum-Rorty was assembling their Essays volume; the two essays were thus produced in mutual independence. Yet substantively, Frede and White CONVERGE on the supervenience thesis: both deny that phantasia is a separate faculty of the soul; both emphasize its derivative/parasitic status on aisthesis; both invoke the De Insomniis formula that phantastikon is the same as aisthetikon but different in being; both stress the kinesis-hypo-aistheseos definition (DA 428b10-11); both treat phantasia as 'preserving' the sensible forms after the sensible object has gone. Where they DIVERGE: White operates within a Thomistic-humanist hermeneutic that culminates in phantasia as 'a familiar interior landscape' orienting man in the cosmos (the heavenly-bodies coda), while Frede operates within an analytic philosophy-of-mind framework that culminates in a polemic against Modrak's unified-consciousness reading and a defence of Aristotelian dualism. White is concerned with phantasia's contribution to the unity of the human soul and to noein's imitation of the divine noetic life; Frede is concerned with phantasia's two cognitive functions (synthesis, bridging) and with the limits of unity. White reads phantasia teleologically toward nous; Frede reads it functionally as a sensory link. The CLUSTER'S TRIANGLE: PHX-01 Nussbaum (expansive practical-rational reading; phantasia as 'envisaging the good'), PHX-02 White (Thomistic-derivative reading; phantasia as preserved sensible forms in service of nous), PHX-03 Frede (minimal supervenience reading; phantasia as parasitic phenomenon with two cognitive functions and dualist boundary). Frede explicitly contests Nussbaum and implicitly converges with White; the cluster's 1985-1992 trajectory shows independent convergence on the supervenience-on-perception thesis from two methodological starting-points (Thomistic close-reading; analytic philosophy of mind), with Nussbaum as the dissenting expansive reading the others are pushing back against.
